column2: Shield Sheafson was a foundling who became a conquering Danish king and forced the clans beyond the sea to pay him tribute.
Beow was Shield Sheafson's son, sent by God to comfort the Danes, and he ruled them well after his father's death.
Halfdane was Beow's heir and Hrothgar's father, a warlord who ruled the Danes for the rest of his life.
Hrothgar is the aging king of the Danes who builds Heorot and suffers helplessly under Grendel's attacks.
Hrothgar once ended a feud for Beowulf's father by paying treasure to the Wulfings, and in return Ecgtheow swore allegiance to him.
Heorogar was Hrothgar's older brother, whom Hrothgar calls the better man, and he died young.
Halga, called "the good," was Hrothgar's younger brother.
Wealhtheow is Hrothgar's queen, who passes the mead cup in order of rank and thanks God for sending Beowulf as a deliverer.

column1: What Wealhtheow asks for her sons
column2: Wealhtheow urges Hrothgar to leave the kingdom to his own kin and asks both Hrothulf and Beowulf to protect her young sons.
Hrethric and Hrothmond are the young sons of Hrothgar and Wealhtheow, between whom Beowulf sits at the victory feast.
Hrothulf is Hrothgar's nephew, whom Wealhtheow trusts to protect her sons, although the poet hints that the Danes will later know feud and betrayal.
Grendel is a man-eating monster descended from Cain who raids Heorot at night because the sounds of feasting and song enrage him.
Grendel had put a spell on every blade, so the swords of Beowulf's men could not wound him.
Cain is the biblical first murderer, and God's curse on him for killing Abel produced a race of monsters that includes Grendel.
Beowulf is a young Geatish warrior of great strength who sails to Denmark to rid Hrothgar's hall of Grendel.
Beowulf arrives already famous for binding beasts, raiding a troll-nest, and killing sea monsters at night.
Ecgtheow is Beowulf's father, a famous warrior who killed Heatholaf and fled to the Danes until Hrothgar paid off the feud.
Hygelac is king of the Geats and Beowulf's lord and uncle, and Beowulf fights Grendel partly to add to Hygelac's fame.
The poet foretells that Hygelac will wear Wealhtheow's torque on a proud raid against the Frisians and die there, leaving his body to the Franks.
Hrethel was the earlier king of the Geats and Beowulf's grandfather, who gave his daughter to Ecgtheow and gave Beowulf his mail shirt.
Weland is the legendary smith who forged the mail shirt that Beowulf wants sent to Hygelac if he dies.
Heatholaf was a warrior of the Wulfings whose killing by Ecgtheow started a feud.
The Wulfings were Heatholaf's tribe, to whom Hrothgar sent treasure to settle their feud with Ecgtheow.
Hrothgar's coast-guard challenges the armed Geats on the beach, judges them honest by their words and bearing, and guides them to Heorot.
Wulfgar is Hrothgar's herald, a Wendel chief, who questions the Geats at the door and persuades Hrothgar to receive them.
Unferth, son of Ecglaf, is a Danish courtier who sits at Hrothgar's feet and, out of envy, mocks Beowulf for losing a swimming match.
Beowulf reveals that Unferth killed his own brothers, a crime that shames him despite his cleverness.
Breca is Beowulf's boyhood rival, who according to Unferth outswam Beowulf in a sea contest and returned home to the Brondings.
The Brondings are Breca's people, to whose country he returned after the swimming match.
The Heathoreams are the people on whose shore the sea cast Breca up after the swim.
The Geats are Beowulf's people, a seafaring tribe of what is now southern Sweden, ruled by Hygelac.
The Danes, also called Shieldings after their founder Shield, are Hrothgar's people, whom Grendel terrorizes for years.
Heorot is Hrothgar's great gold-roofed mead-hall, where Grendel kills Danes until Beowulf defends it.
Geatland is Beowulf's homeland across the sea from Denmark, where Hygelac rules.
Hrothgar's poet sings of God's creation of the world in Heorot, a song that angers Grendel.

column1: The scop on the ride back
column2: A thane skilled in old stories composes new verses on Beowulf's victory and compares him to famous heroes.
Sigemund is a legendary hero whose dragon-slaying and treasure-winning the scop sings about to praise Beowulf by comparison.
Fitela is Sigemund's nephew and battle partner, who was absent when Sigemund killed the dragon.
Heremod is a Danish king whom the scop contrasts with Beowulf, because evil entered him and he became a burden to his people.
Finn is the Frisian king in the scop's lay whose truce with the Danes breaks down, and he is killed in his own hall.
Hnaef is the Danish leader killed in the fight in Friesland, whose body is burned on one pyre with his nephew's.
Hildeburh is Finn's queen, who loses both her brother Hnaef and her son in the fight and has them burned together.
Hengest takes command of the Danes after Hnaef's death, spends a bitter winter with Finn, and finally takes revenge.
The Frisians are Finn's people, whose forced truce with the Danes ends in revenge and the sack of Finn's hall.
The Jutes are the enemies in the Finn story whom Hildeburh has little cause to trust and whom Hengest longs to repay.
Hunlafing lays a famous sword on Hengest's lap, a gesture that pushes Hengest to break the truce and take revenge.
Guthlaf and Oslaf are Danes who return from a voyage and blame Finn for the ambush, which leads to his killing.
Hama is a legendary hero who carried off the Brosings' necklace from Eormenric, and the poet uses him to praise the torque Wealhtheow gives Beowulf.
Seamus Heaney was the Irish poet whose modern English translation of Beowulf keeps the poem's alliteration and adds Irish words like "bawn."
The Beowulf poet was an unknown Christian author in England who wrote down an older pagan story about Scandinavian heroes.
